content.summary_of_the_paper: this submission deals with progressive dimensionality reduction of diffusion models for high resolution image synthesis. To destroy the signal, the signal projection onto an orthogonal basis is progressively attenuated until left with pure noise. To reverse the process, the signal is approximately reconstructed from the low dimensional observations. Experiments with different datasets show superior FID to DDPM for high resolution (up to 1024x1024) synthesis.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- The idea is solid; the progressive attenuation of the signal basis is a well grounded idea
the considered problem of dimensionality reduction for diffusions is an important problem

Weakness
- The significance of the work is not clear given other approaches such as subspace diffusion, pyramid diffusions, and latent diffusions addressing dimensionality reduction;  in particular, latent diffusions have been trying to leverage low dimensionality of images. However, no comparisons are made in the paper


Questions and comments
- How does one decide about the compression operator U? A discussion or ablation about the choice of orthogonal basis with their trade offs, is useful for the readership. Can one simply use a data driven PCA per sample?

- A discussion/ablation on the degree that one can compress, i.e., K, would be useful for high resolution synthesis of diverse datasets such as LSUN or ImageNet. Apparently 4x downsampling is used in the paper as the default, but what would be the trade off if one chooses a large downsampling factor?

- How would the progressive attenuation work for conditional generation such as super-resolution when the input conditioning is not in the same dimension as the reduced dimensionality diffusion? comments along this line would be useful.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written. The progressive dimensionality reduction idea is also novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a timely topic. The progressive attenuation idea is also solid and relevant for dimensionality reduction. The significance of the work is not however significant, in terms of computational saving and quality, compared with SOTA methods. This work also needs comparison with latent diffusions that aim to leverage the low dimensionality of images. In addition, further ablations are needed to demonstrate the reduction capability of this method for high resolution generation and diverse datasets that FFHQ such as LSUN and ImageNet.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a diffusion-based generative architecture based on a multi-resolution diffusion process. In particular, during every few hundred iterations of the diffusion process the resolution of the image is reduced, such that eventually all that remains is a 16x16 noise image. By allowing many iterations of the reverse process to operate at lower resolution, the proposed method reduces both training and inference times by about 2x. The method enables effective 1024x1024 FFHQ image synthesis.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths
The proposed idea is interesting and well-motivated.

The paper successfully demonstrates 1024x1024 image synthesis.

Paper reducing training and inference costs associated with diffusion models by about 2x.

The paper provides theoretical bounds on the approximation error associated with the multiscale diffusion process.

# Weaknesses
While the paper cites Rombach et al's stable diffusion paper [A] as evidence standard diffusion models are slow, it provides no comparisons with this method nor does the paper acknowledge that stable diffusion has overlapping ideas. For example, the paper states "We therefore argue that there is no need to follow the source signal dimensions along the entire distribution evolution process". Stable diffusion leverages the same insight in operating in the latent space (although the dimensions were fixed in this case).
[A] Rombach, Robin, et al. "High-resolution image synthesis with latent diffusion models." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.

The paper has very few comparisons and should likely avoid claiming the proposed method is state-of-the-art. (The 256x256 FID scores reported in [A] for many different architectures, e.g., ProjectedGAN [B],  were far better than the results reported in this work. Similarly StyleGAN-XL [C] reported an FID of 2.02 on the FFHQ 1024^2 dataset -- the current method's FID is 15.07.)
[B] Sauer, A., Chitta, K., Müller, J., & Geiger, A. (2021). Projected gans converge faster. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 34, 17480-17492.
[C] Sauer, Axel, Katja Schwarz, and Andreas Geiger. "Stylegan-xl: Scaling stylegan to large diverse datasets." ACM SIGGRAPH 2022 Conference Proceedings. 2022.


The paper reports the training time associated with training 256x256 models, but not 1024x1024 models. This is frustrating as the papers main contribution is scaling training to higher resolutions.

The paper doesn't compare overall training costs with other methods (e.g., [A]) at 1024x1024.

The paper has several minor grammatical errors and typos.
pg 5: "compensate the" --> "compensate for the"
pg 5: "Gaussians that" --> "Gaussians such that"
pg 8: "downsamling" --> "downsampling"
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
While certain sections can be dense and hard to read, overall the paper is clear enough. 

The quality of the proposed method does not seem comparable to recent methods such as [A] and [C] and the paper is missing important comparisons.

The multiscale diffusion process is, to my knowledge, novel.

While there's not much info about the architecture in the text (the paper could benefit from a larger supplement), the abstract says code will be made available.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the proposed idea is interesting, well-motivated, and somewhat effective in reducing diffusion model computational costs, the paper is let down by its lack of comparisons. The paper does not demonstrate it advances the state-of-the-art.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to generalize the diffusion models to learning a dimensionality-varying process, where the forward diffusion and reverse diffusiondo not happen in the original data space at all timesteps. Specifically, the during forward process, some components of the clean images are "attenuated" toward zero, learning to the possibility of dropping these inconsequential components. In addition to the theoretical guarantee, the authors also provide extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strong points

- The paper proposes a framework of dimensional-varying diffusion models to accelerate and improve the original diffusion models.

- The paper analyzes the incurred error of dimension-varying during training and sampling.

- Experimentally, the proposed method improves over baselines in terms of sample quality and sampling speed, especially on higher resolution image datasets.


### Weak points


- The paper is not clearly written. The actual training and sampling algorithms need to be highlighted in the main text. Currently, it is not clear how to develop the algorithms based on text. For example, how to get/calculate the subspace, their corresponding orthonormal basis $u_{i,1}, …, u_{K,d_K}$, the orthogonal vectors $v_0, …,v_K$, the parameter $\bar{\lambda}_{i,t}$, and how to (principally) choose when to attenuate.

- To the best of my understanding, the proposed method and subspace diffusion both do 2x2 average pooling as the downsampling operator, and the forward process runs in the given downsampled subspace. To gain dimension during sampling time, they also add Gaussian noise (orthogonal to the subspace) to the upsampled images. If I am wrong I am happy to be corrected (this also relates to item 3 below).

- The mentioning of the existing subspace diffusion paper needs to be done sooner, as it has the same motivation and a very similar if not the same approach. The comparison between the proposed method and subspace diffusion also needs to be made more thoroughly and clearly. Currently, they are only compared in one experimental setting on CelebA $64^2$ and none in theory. The authors only vaguely claim that they "lack a proper method to supplement the loss of high-frequency information at the moment of variation" in Sections 4.3 and 5. This claim is also listed as the main contribution in Section 5, which I struggle to locate in the paper. With the current way of writing the theory, it is hard to tell the difference between the two approaches. I would like to see the proposed method more thoroughly compared with subspace diffusion both in theory and in practice (performance and sampling time), if not in the main text, then at least in Appendix.

- There are quite large gaps between theory and practice for the proposed method. Besides the points mentioned above, for example, in section 3.3, the error analysis is made under the condition that the attenuation parameters $\bar{\lambda}_{i,t}$ approximate 0, but in practice, the downsampling timesteps seem to be chosen arbitrarily and no analysis of whether the aforementioned conditions actually hold in practice was done.

- The practical value of the paper is unclear. As the author correctly points out, there is great redundancy in the early generation phase, which allows many numerical methods to take larger step sizes. As far as I know, several papers can achieve 10x - 20x speed-up (current paper is around 1.3x-2.4x) by improving the sampling process, such as DDIM, DPM-solver or DEIS.


### Other comments or questions:

- The author uses  "the average number of iterations per second estimated over 4,000 iterations" to measure the training speed. It's more nature to use the required wall-clock training time to obtain the best performance model (or convergence).

- In Section 5, the authors claim that subspace diffusion is limited in terms of the number of dimensionality variations. I am not sure about this claim. It is true that in their experiments, they only changed once, but their method and theory allow for multiple time downsampling.

- In Table 1, CIFAR10 should be labeled as $32^2$.

- In Theorem 1, it seems that the JSD term ($\xi_1$ ) must include $q(x_t)$.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The differences and connections with similar previous work (subspace) are not properly discussed in this paper. The main text is tangent to the experimental section: many concepts developed in the main text are no longer used in the actual training and sampling. This work has limited novelty, since it's quite similar to the previous subspace work.
content.summary_of_the_review: There are quite large gaps between theory and practice for the proposed method. The current version is very similar to a previous work. In addition, the utility of dimensional reduction is questionable. The reviewer leans toward rejection for the current version.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The work presented in this paper aims at defining a new type of diffusion processes, by which the dimensionality of the “latent” space decreases as time progresses in the forward process, and consequently, increases in the backward process, starting from a low-dimensional noise sample. This is achieved by decomposing the original input into a series of orthogonal components, which is implemented through a max-pooling operation and a down-sampling function.
Formally, the forward and backward process are defined through the lenses of an approximate transition kernel that can be reversed (by overcoming some challenges), leading to a similar form of the optimisation objective as for a DDPM model. An error analysis complements the formalisation of the forward and backward diffusion process, whereby the authors state that the approximation error goes to zero.
A series of experiments on 6 datasets complement the proposed method, whereby the authors show that the generative quality they obtain is on par, and sometimes superior to alternatives, with smaller training and sampling costs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strong point of this work are:

* The idea of a compression of the latent space throughout the diffusion process is truly needed. This could open up an interesting direction of research akin to “an information bottleneck” for diffusion processes

* The experimental section is thorough and demonstrates how the proposed method compares to several alternatives from the state of the art

* The error analysis is a necessary step to validate the applicability of the proposed model, and the paper presents a valid attempt at indicating the approximation gap induced by the proposed methodology vanishes

The weak points are:

* Lack of clarity in mathematical notation, and exposition of the proposed method. If, on the one hand, I could get the gist of the idea, how to implement it, and what is the main pain-point (the reverse process), on the other hand reading section 3 is daunting.

* One of the main problem arise after eq.(6), where two concepts of time appear: one is the time evolution of the diffusion process, the other is a “virtual” time induced by the original and latent space decomposition. We thus end up with two “time” indexes which is really confusing to me.

* The introduction of a “turning point” can also be improved: intuitively, this is the time $T_k$ such that $x_t$ can be approximated by a subspace version of it, namely $x_{k,t}$, by neglecting all terms that “vanish”. I think that Fig.3 is not very helpful, as I am not sure I see orthogonal vectors except for the first subfigure. Another aspect that is not clearly explained is the equivalence between dropping noise terms vs. compensating them. This is **the key** aspect to consider in the reverse process.

* Also the reverse process is very hard to follow. To begin, the reason why it is not possible “to step over $T_k$“ should be better elaborated, maybe relating to the singularity properties of the matrices involved in the process. The difficulty lies in the fact that we need to go from $y_{k,T_k}$ to $y_{k-1, T_k}$, which have different dimensions, and to do so the authors propose to inject noise of the same dimension of $y_{k-1, T_k}$. Do we also need to upsample $y_{k,T_k}$? Why do we have a downsample operator, but not an upsample one?

* The denoising loss “look-a-like” in eq.(15) is presented without appropriate explanation. I am afraid that this does not stem from a valid ELBO for the model, and I would like the authors to develop more on the approach to arrive at the proposed loss. I also think there is a typo, as you may want to work on the *squared* 2-norm.

* Finally, concerning the error analysis that attempts at showing that both the forward and backward processes approximations vanish, I am left wondering (at the intuitive level), how is this even possible. When we decompose the original signal into orthogonal components, we use a “destructive” operation that is average pooling. If we kept all of the subspaces, we may be able to recover the original signal. However, since we discard components, I am not sure that the approximation error goes to zero. When I read Theorem 1 and 2, and glance over the proofs, I see why it could work. For example, in the forward process, we try to show that the approximation error between an error compensated variant of $x_{k,t}$, that is $\tilde{x_{k,t}}$, and $x_t$ goes to zero, because of the noise compensation. But then the final claim is to say that *``the difference between the real distribution of $x_t$ and the approximated distribution $x_{k,t}$ goes to zero’’*, which is not the same as the noise compensated distribution. I think that a better intuitive explanation would be very helpful.

* Experiments: I have several questions that are connected to the theory questions above. How do you decide the preset values of diffusion time to decide that it is OK to decrease the latent size? From theory, we should check the values of $\hat{\lambda}_{i,t}$, and make sure we compensate for noise, whereas in the experiments, the values in the set $\hat{T}$ seem to be set heuristically. Can you clarify?

* Experiments: acceleration of both training and sampling. While the results presented, for example, in Table 1 and Table 3 indicate that the proposed method indeed provides speed up in both cases, other work that is not mentioned in the related literature also dramatically decreases training and sampling times. For example, latent diffusion models (that is cited in the introduction), and the work presented in [1] enjoy dramatic improvements because they operate on a smaller dimensionality than the original input domain. 
So a natural question is in order: if we believe that working on lower dimensionality spaces is beneficial for diffusion models, what is the main advantage of the proposed method when compared to an approach that “compresses” the input domain before diffusion, and that “decompresses” the reverse diffusion process?
I think this question should be addressed in various ways: 1) motivations for the proposed method, 2) theoretical justification of the proposed method, 3) experimental comparison with a latent diffusion model (even a simpler version whereby the “compression” and “decompression” is done with a simple, pre-trained autoencoder instead of a jointly trained variational autoencoder as done in stable diffusion).

[1] @misc{https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2106.05931,
  url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05931},
  author = {Vahdat, Arash and Kreis, Karsten and Kautz, Jan},
  title = {Score-based Generative Modeling in Latent Space},
  publisher = {arXiv},
  year = {2021},
}
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I had a very hard time reading this paper, due to the heavy mathematical notation and to the convoluted prose. I think the authors did a tremendous amount of work, and that the quality suffers from the exposition. On the novelty side, I think the proposed approach is novel, and well positioned with respect to related work. 
However, I think a key question should be answered: what is the advantage of the proposed method when compared to an alternative approach that directly works on a smaller “latent space” obtained by encoding the input domain? Why do we need to gradually decrease the input size during the diffusion process, with the difficulties that this entails, when we could directly “jump” to a small space from the start?
Finally, concerning reproducibility, I think this work will definitely require code to be shared, as its formulation is not very simple and as a consequence I suspect the implementation will not be straightforward. On the empirical side, I would also like to learn about effective strategies to select the set of down-sampling times $\hat{T}$.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This work presents a method whose goal is to reduce the dimensionality of the latent variables that arise during the diffusion process, and sample from a low-dimensional noise distribution to go bag, gradually to the original input domain dimension. The motivation to do so are mainly two: 1) computational efficiency in training and sampling, 2) the possibility to generate high-resolution images from low-dimensional noise samples.
Besides the editorial quality and mathematical notation, that can be improved by polishing the paper, and the several questions related to the inner workings of the proposed approach, I think the most pressing question to answer is how does this method compare to the existing alternative of working directly in a small-dimension space obtained by first encoding the input, and then decoding the result of the reverse diffusion.

content.title: Dimensionality-Varying Diffusion Process
content.abstract: Diffusion models, which learn to reverse a signal destruction process to generate new data, typically require the signal at each step to have the same dimension. We argue that, considering the spatial redundancy in image signals, there is no need to maintain a high dimensionality in the evolution process, especially in the early generation phase. To this end, we make a theoretical generalization of the forward diffusion process via signal decomposition. Concretely, we manage to decompose an image into multiple orthogonal components and control the attenuation of each component when perturbing the image. That way, along with the noise strength increasing, we are able to diminish those inconsequential components and thus use a lower-dimensional signal to represent the source, barely losing information. Such a reformulation allows to vary dimensions in both training and inference of diffusion models. Extensive experiments on a range of datasets suggest that our approach substantially reduces the computational cost and achieves on-par or even better synthesis performance compared to baseline method.We also show that our strategy facilitates high-resolution image synthesis and improves FID of diffusion model trained on FFHQ at $1024\times1024$ resolution from 52.40 to 15.07. Code and models will be made publicly available.
